title: Event-driven architecture
idea: Event-driven architecture is a design where a service publishes an event, a record that something happened, and other services react on their own.

analogy.text: A shop-floor announcement: "Order 7 is paid." Packing, billing and delivery each hear it and act. The announcer never assigns the work.
analogy.breaks: A spoken announcement is lost if missed; a broker can keep events.

points: The publisher emits an event and moves on; it does not call anyone.
A broker receives events and delivers each one to every subscribed service.
Consumers react independently, so you add a new one without touching the publisher.
The cost: effects arrive later, and no single call chain shows the whole flow.

steps.caption: A customer places an order. The Orders service saves it.
Orders publishes `OrderPlaced`. It names no receiver, and it replies to the customer at once.
The broker delivers a copy to every service subscribed to `OrderPlaced`.
Each consumer reacts on its own: a receipt, a stock reservation, an invoice.
Inventory goes down. The next order is still accepted and published as before.
A durable broker keeps the event for Inventory. Email and Billing carry on.
Inventory restarts, receives the waiting event and catches up. The publisher never knew.

code.title: A tiny pub/sub
code.caption: Add a third `bus.on` listener: `placeOrder` does not change. Unlike a real broker, `EventEmitter` runs listeners synchronously, in one process.

pitfalls: Use a direct call, not an event, when the caller needs the answer now.
Assume an event can arrive twice; make each consumer safe to run again (idempotent, see queues).
Treat event fields as a contract; renaming one silently breaks consumers you cannot see.

quiz.why: A listener only hears events emitted after it subscribes. The first emit reached email alone; the second reached both.

takeaway: Publish what happened; let other services decide how to react.
